I worked (with Claude, of course) on a human readable document that explains the core ideas of the consistency proof behind con-leche, and why these annotations help to push the proof through:

  • HTML: https://leanprover.github.io/con-leche/con-leche-proof-idea.html
  • PDF: https://leanprover.github.io/con-leche/con-leche-proof-idea.pdf

This is written by Claude, then reviewed by me, and iterated upon.

The TL;DR behind the proof idea may be this:

Such a consistency proof needs some form of “preservation”: If you reduce a redex in a well-typed input, you get something well-typed. For that you (usually) need that the argument of the redex has the same type as the lambda’s parameter. You could just do that type-check at runtime, but that would be slow. You could work on fully annotated terms (i.e. derivations), then the types to compare are right there, but still expensive. You could get that check by inversion from “input is well-typed”, but that needs sufficient good meta-theory, which is hard to get.

So con-leche mixes and matches: It annotates the terms not with the full type, but just whether the codomain is always a type or possibly a prop. If it is a type, the inversion on our “well-typed”-like predicate works. If it is not always a type, we do the runtime check.

Anyways, I hope this write up is useful to someone, in addition to me (it was for me). Feedback welcome, I can do a few more rounds of refinements.)
Do you know why it did not opt to define an extensional type theory?

That was actually my starting point, also given that I wanted to build on inductives-models: define an ETT, map Lean into it, prove the ETT consistent with a set model. But the last step didn't work: because of extensionality and propext, if I remember correctly, we couldn't have the injectivity of Pi and the beta reduction wouldn't go through. So (after a fair number of wild attempts and dead ends) we cut the middleman (the ETT) and aimed at the direct proof.
Huh, I don't need injectivity of pi in my set theory model in metalean

I thought your type theory in the middle is not extensional?

I assume your consistency proof is by inductions on typing derivations, i.e. no syntax driven interpretation of just terms into sets?
Just induction on the typing derivation yes

I don't see why extensionality would make the proof substantially different, especially to require pi injectivity, which I find strange, since pi injectivity obviously does not hold in extensional type theory
Could be worth another attempt at ETT
Try it! A nice ETT type system as a target would be very useful, because we could add and explain more features this way.

As just mentioned in #general > con-leche, a lean checker with a proof of consistency @ 💬 I have re-done the consistency proof in a way that doesn't need the “prop when” annotation on binders.

The proof idea write-up at https://leanprover.github.io/con-leche/con-leche-proof-idea.html is updated. The Tl;DR is as follows:

The crux is that

  • I want a syntax-driven interpretation into set. This is different from the conventional proofs with a declarative type system in between, where the model may be defined over derivations and thus has much more information at hand.
  • A propositions is either ∅\emptyset∅ or {∙}\{\bullet\}{∙}, and every proof must be ∙\bullet∙
  • Lean’s ∀ can be either a (non-prop) type or a proposition.

The previous version of con-leche used the annotation to disambiguate. The current version disambiguates based on the semantic value: If all the values of the function are ∙\bullet∙, i.e. look like a proof, then the denotation of the function is ∙\bullet∙, else it is a proper function in the usual set theoretic way.

This does the right thing for propositions, and also for function types with non-empty domain. But for Empty → …, there is no value to look at, and the interpretation cannot know whether … is a type or a prop. So vacuously such functions become ∙\bullet∙ as well.

This causes slight issues. In order to prove the β rule sound, we need to know from [f a] being ok that [a] really lies in the domain of [f]. For normal functions that works, but not if [f]=∙ = \bullet=∙.

I had actually tried this route (the “collapsed model”) before I had tried the annotations and got the first working proof. So why does it work now? Because now I only expect reduction to be doing the right thing under the assumption that the term we start with isn't ∙\bullet∙. And that works out: Proofs we don’t want to reduce anyways (and if we do it doesn't really matter what happens to them), and for these “empty functions” the argument works quite similarly.

This leaves surprisingly few places in the checker code where the proof against this model does not go through, primarily defeq checking between two lambdas. And here we can pay a bit of “certification tax” to get the proof go through: In addition to checking that the bodies are defeq, we also infer their types and check that the types are defeq. These extra premises are blue in https://leanprover.github.io/con-leche/con-leche-proof-idea.html#loc-9.

Not sure if anyone cares about the details of this proof but me, but if you do, please have a look at https://leanprover.github.io/con-leche/con-leche-proof-idea.html and also let me know where this text wasn't as helpful to you as it could have been.

I'm currently making my way through the paper.

After a few hours I made it through the first paragraph (yay!), but now I'm stuck on the second paragraph. I would like to ask for some clarification about my confusion.

In the write up, it says "The theorem is relative to a model of an abstract set theory, a structure with membership, extensionality, the usual set-forming operations and a chain of universes closed under them". This seems to be claiming that con-leche gives a proof of

Con(ZFC_omega) => [con-leche checker accepts no proof of False].

But it seems like the true set-theoretic assumptions used are actually stronger. Namely, the con-leche proof uses the Lean type theory PLUS a tower of universes on top of a model set theory intrinsic to Lean. So if you expect Lean to already need ZFC_omega to model it's universes, then con-leche's "Lean + tower of universes within it" assumption seems like it would need an even larger cardinal axiom if you wanted to write it in pure set theory, like a tower of towers.
[Just as a set-theory reminder cause I was confused for a while: ZFC_{omega+omega} is strictly stronger than ZFC_omega, even though omega+omega and omega are both countable]

[Also, when you wrote this all out in set theory, there's a good chance you can do it all in ZFC_omega though it's not 100% clear. It seems like the con-leche proof only uses finite levels, i.e., ZFC_n for all finite n. Working with these finite levels you might expect that you only need the consistency of ZFC_{n+m} for every finite n,m, which is implied by a single tower, ZFC_omega]

For what it is worth, I think the natural way this should be stated is if M is a model of first order ZFC + {n inaccessibles | n in omega} then con leche can’t prove false. (By completeness theorem this is same as con(ZFC + {n inaccessibles | n in omega}) -> con leche can’t prove false.) it should not use second order ZFC. I tried to fix the con leche proof of this over the summer, but Leanstral wasn’t powerful enough. Let me try again with a different model. This formulation is also nice because it also lets you prove if phi is a statement of arithmetic and con leche proves phi them M models phi. (And maybe one can also do what @Milo Moses is saying about giving the more precise version with finitely many universe levels.)

Jason Rute said:

This formulation is also nice because it also lets you prove if phi is a statement of arithmetic and con leche proves phi them M models phi.

I think this point is important and it's something that I would like to see highlighted in con-leche. There's this question about how to interpret Lean theorems in usual set theory. For statements about arithmetic, what @Jason Rute is saying is a good approach. But there's some subtle statements in mathlib where in my mind it's unclear how to convert between the statement in Lean and the statement in plain set theory (such as the Freyd-Mitchell embedding theorem).

The con-leche project is subtle/interesting/delicate because it doesn't construct a "type theory" in the classical sense. When I think of "type theory", the central notion is that you have a thing called a type and a thing called a term, and having a well-defined typing judgement which is independent of any specific algorithm you used to verify that typing judgement.

In con-leche, you have explicitly given this up. You no longer have a type theory; you have checker whose acceptance/rejectance judgements share a lot of metamathematical properties that are similar to a type theory. The checker builds a set theoretic model for every Lean environment, but that set theoretic model depends on the specific route the checker took.

If you had a standard type theory for Lean 4 and you proved that it was consistent that would be great, and consistency is mostly the only thing you need to show.

For con-leche, you need more than just a proof that the checker does not accept False. There are other a metamathematical properties you need to formulate and prove. The con-leche repository has formalized some of these other metamathematical properties and proved them, but it's not clear to me if what is has done is correct/sufficient. I'll need to keep checking closely.

Milo Moses schrieb:

It seems like the con-leche proof only uses finite levels, i.e., ZFC_n for all finite n.

Yes, and you could even go a step further and do a meta-theoretical argument that for every concrete proof you have to check, you really only need number finite levels. I think @Cameron Zwarich discussed this in some other thread with more detail, I’l defer to th eexpertes here.

Although I am surprised that this intermediate layer of a “declarative type system” is so important to many people. To me, when I write math in Lean, I think of sets, and Lean’s syntax and type system is just a convenience to not get lost in the untyped world of sets, but in the end I (intuitively) am defining mathematial objects as sets and proving things about them. For that I don’t need the intermediate typing judgement, I just need that the interpretatoin of Lean terms in sets matches what I expect.

Joachim Breitner said:

I just need that the interpretatoin of Lean terms in sets matches what I expect.

100% agree, this should be the goal of a metamathematical theory of Lean. A semantic interpretation of Lean statements in set theory which matches what Lean practitioners have learned to expect [though again examples like Freyd-Mitchell embedding showcases that there are settings where this is subtle].
